h1: What goes into a winery business plan
title: Winery Business Plan: What to Include | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical outline of a winery business plan: market, fruit, production, cash flow, people and risks, plus what an investor or bank looks for.
teaser: A winery plan that only describes the wine is half a plan. The other half is cash, timing and who buys.
standfirst: A business plan for a winery has to deal with a product that is made once a year and sold over several. Here is what each section should hold and where plans usually go thin.
sections: Start with the idea in plain words
Open with a short summary: what you will make, for whom, at what price and how you will reach them. A reader should know your business after one page. Detail belongs later.

Say who buys your wine and why they would pick yours over the bottle next to it. Use real evidence: conversations with shop buyers, restaurant managers and tasting-room visitors, price checks on the shelf plus tasting feedback. Our guide on market research for a new wine brand shows how to gather it.

Avoid unsourced claims that the market is growing. Investors have read them many times.

Describe where the fruit comes from, the varieties or fruits, the style of wine and the approach to fermentation, ageing and bottling. State your capacity in bottles per year and what limits it: tank space, fruit supply, labour or bottling.

Name who makes the wine. A plan with no experienced winemaker is a risk the reader will notice at once.
Operations, licences and the production calendar

Cover the site, buildings, equipment, water and power, waste handling and staff. Add the licensing path and who is responsible for it. Rules differ by country and by Indian state and they change, so show that you know which approvals are needed and have asked the authority or an adviser.

Show the winery's year on one page. Harvest and crush, fermentation, racking, ageing, bottling and release each take time and each needs cash and labour at a known point. A simple calendar makes it obvious when you need extra hands, when tanks are full and when money is tight.

It also shows a lender that you understand the product. Wine is a slow business and a plan that shows the clock is more credible than one that does not.

List each channel with its price, margin and the effort it takes: tasting room, shops, restaurants, club, online where allowed and export. A bottle sold from your own door earns a different margin from one sold through a distributor. Show the mix you expect in the first three years and why.

Keep marketing within local alcohol advertising rules and never aim it at minors.

This is the part most winery plans get wrong. Include:

  • Start-up costs, split into building, equipment, licences, fees and working capital.
  • A monthly cash flow for at least the first two years, showing harvest costs, ageing time and when sales cash arrives.
  • A profit and loss account by year.
  • Break-even volume.
  • A sensitivity test: what happens if fruit costs rise, a vintage is smaller or sales arrive six months late.

For a small illustration, suppose a winery spends 100 units on a vintage in autumn and sells the wine over the following 18 months. The cash is gone in month one and returns slowly. A plan that shows only annual profit hides that gap. See why ageing ties up cash.

These are hypothetical numbers for the method. Use your own.
Risks, people and a last check

Name the real risks: a poor harvest, a faulty batch, a delayed licence, a slow channel. Say what you would do about each. Then show the team and their experience. Banks and investors back people as much as wine.

Before you finish the document, check it against a short list. Can you state your price per bottle on each channel? Do you know your cost per bottle? Can you say how many months of cash you need between picking and payment? Do you know who the first ten buyers are? If any answer is vague, the plan is not ready for a reader.

Our guide on working out cost per bottle helps with the second question.

Plans for wineries tend to fail in a few places. Capacity is stated without checking the bottleneck. Sales are assumed to arrive in the year the wine is made. Fruit cost is treated as fixed when it is not. Staff for the tasting room are forgotten. Licence timing is guessed.

A careful reader looks for these first. Fix them before the plan goes out and the conversation will be about the opportunity rather than the gaps.
faqs: How long should a winery business plan be?
Long enough to answer a reader's questions and short enough to be read, with a one-page summary at the front. The spreadsheet matters more than the prose.
What do banks look for in a winery plan?
Cash flow that covers the ageing period, a realistic sales route, experienced people and security. See our guide on funding a winery.
Is a business plan the same as a project report?
They overlap. A project report, often called a DPR in India, is more detailed on technical and cost figures and is usually written for a lender or authority.
Yes, but the financial model is where outside help pays for itself.
